lessonTitle: Infection Prevention in Practice: Hand Hygiene, Isolation Precautions and Outbreak Control

blocks.text: On a surgical ward, five patients in a fortnight develop the same watery diarrhoea. Nobody has done anything obviously wrong, and every patient was seen by many staff. Whether the ward is a victim of one contaminated source or of a hundred missed hand-washes is exactly the kind of question infection prevention exists to answer.

blocks.markdown: Most healthcare-associated infections are spread by **contact**, especially on the hands of staff, and many are preventable. Infection prevention rests on three layers: **standard precautions** applied to every patient, **transmission-based precautions** added when an infection is known or suspected, and a structured **outbreak investigation** when cases cluster.

blocks.title: Standard precautions
blocks.text: Basic infection control measures applied to all patients at all times, regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) based on risk of exposure to blood and body fluids, safe handling of sharps, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, environmental cleaning, and safe management of linen and waste.

blocks.markdown: **Hand hygiene: the five moments** (World Health Organization). Clean hands at: (1) **before touching a patient**; (2) **before a clean or aseptic procedure**; (3) **after body fluid exposure risk**; (4) **after touching a patient**; (5) **after touching patient surroundings**. Moments 1 and 2 protect the patient from organisms on the hands; moments 3 to 5 protect the healthcare worker and the next patient. **Alcohol-based hand rub** is the preferred method when hands are not visibly soiled because it is fast and kills most bacteria and enveloped viruses. **Soap and water** is required when hands are visibly dirty and in outbreaks of *Clostridioides difficile* (spores resist alcohol) and of norovirus (alcohol is less reliable against this non-enveloped virus).

blocks.title: Which hand-hygiene moment applies?
blocks.prompt: A nurse puts on gloves to flush a peripheral venous cannula, having just adjusted the patient's bed table. Identify the moments for hand hygiene.

steps.text: She has touched the patient's surroundings, then will perform a clean procedure on the cannula: moment 5 applies after touching the surroundings and moments 1 and 2 apply before touching the patient and starting the procedure.
The key moment for protecting the patient is moment 2, immediately before the aseptic task, since the cannula gives a direct route into the bloodstream.
After finishing, if she has touched the patient, moment 4 applies; if body fluid exposure occurred, moment 3 applies.

blocks.answer: Clean hands before touching the patient and, crucially, immediately before the aseptic cannula procedure (moment 2).

blocks.markdown: Compliance is audited by direct observation: the proportion of observed opportunities in which hand hygiene was performed correctly. Auditing with feedback is a proven way to improve adherence.

blocks.caption: Standard audit measure for hand hygiene

blocks.markdown: **Transmission-based precautions** are added to standard precautions according to the route of spread. **Contact**: direct or indirect touch (for example MRSA, *C. difficile*, norovirus); gloves and apron, a single room, dedicated equipment. **Droplet**: large respiratory particles (greater than about 5 micrometres) expelled by coughing or sneezing that travel a short distance (about 1-2 metres) and settle quickly (influenza, meningococcal infection, pertussis); a surgical mask for staff within close range and a single room. **Airborne**: tiny droplet nuclei (less than about 5 micrometres) that stay suspended and travel over long distances (tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox); a negative-pressure single room and a fitted filtering respirator (FFP3 or N95) for staff.

blocks.caption: Transmission-based precautions
rows: Gloves and apron, single room, dedicated equipment, soap and water for C. difficile
Surgical mask, single room, respiratory hygiene

blocks.markdown: **Investigating an outbreak.** An **outbreak** is two or more linked cases, or a greater-than-expected number of cases, in a place and time. Typical steps: (1) **confirm** that there is an outbreak and verify the diagnosis; (2) **define a case** (clinical, time, place and person criteria); (3) **find cases** actively; (4) **describe** the cases by time (epidemic curve), place and person; (5) form a **hypothesis** about source and route; (6) **implement control measures** immediately without waiting for proof, such as isolation, cohorting, cleaning and stopping the suspected source; (7) test the hypothesis by an **analytic study** (for example comparing exposures in cases and controls) and by laboratory **typing** of isolates; (8) **communicate** findings and review the response.

blocks.title: Attack rate on a ward
blocks.prompt: In a ward outbreak of diarrhoea, 14 of 35 patients present during the week become ill. Calculate the attack rate and say what it measures.

steps.text: Attack rate = cases divided by population at risk.

blocks.answer: 40%: the proportion of those exposed who became ill, which helps quantify the scale of the outbreak.

items: Confirm the outbreak and the diagnosis.
Define a case and find further cases.
Describe by time, place and person.
Test the hypothesis, type isolates and communicate.

blocks.title: Act before you are certain
blocks.text: Control measures start as soon as an outbreak is suspected. Waiting for definitive laboratory proof allows further patients to be infected.

blocks.title: Alcohol rub is not always enough
blocks.text: Alcohol gel does not reliably kill C. difficile spores or norovirus and does not remove visible dirt. In those settings use soap and water, and keep standard precautions in place alongside transmission-based ones.

points: Standard precautions apply to every patient; transmission-based precautions are added for contact, droplet or airborne spread.
The five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings.
Airborne spread needs a negative-pressure room and a fitted respirator; droplet needs a surgical mask; contact needs gloves and apron.
Outbreak investigation: confirm, define cases, find cases, describe, hypothesise, control, test, communicate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the five moments for hand hygiene?

options.text: Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Before entering the hospital building
After writing in the notes at the nurses' station
Once at the start of each shift

questions.correctOptionText: Before a clean or aseptic procedure

distractorRationale.b: Not one of the five moments.
distractorRationale.c: Hand hygiene is required after touching the patient or surroundings, not after paperwork away from the patient zone.
distractorRationale.d: Hygiene is tied to patient-care events, not to the shift.

questions.explanation: The five moments are tied to patient contact and risk: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching surroundings. Hand hygiene before aseptic work is the moment that most directly protects the patient.

questions.stem: During an outbreak of Clostridioides difficile infection on a ward, which hand hygiene method is preferred after contact with a patient?

options.text: Washing with soap and water, because alcohol does not reliably kill spores
Alcohol hand rub only, because it is faster
No hand hygiene is needed if gloves were worn
Alcohol hand rub twice

questions.correctOptionText: Washing with soap and water, because alcohol does not reliably kill spores

distractorRationale.b: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. difficile spores.
distractorRationale.c: Hands must still be cleaned after glove removal.
distractorRationale.d: Repeating alcohol rub does not overcome spore resistance.

questions.explanation: Spores resist alcohol, and washing physically removes them from the hands. Gloves are an additional barrier, not a replacement for hand hygiene.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted with a cough, weight loss and a cavity on chest radiograph; pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which precautions are appropriate?

options.text: Airborne precautions: negative-pressure single room and a fitted filtering respirator for staff
Contact precautions only: gloves and apron
Droplet precautions only: surgical mask and an open bay
Standard precautions only, because TB is not transmissible

questions.correctOptionText: Airborne precautions: negative-pressure single room and a fitted filtering respirator for staff

distractorRationale.b: TB is not mainly spread by contact.
distractorRationale.c: Surgical masks do not reliably filter droplet nuclei, and an open bay exposes others.
distractorRationale.d: Pulmonary TB is transmissible by the airborne route.

questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is spread by small droplet nuclei that remain suspended in air. Airborne precautions require a negative-pressure room and a fitted respirator.

questions.stem: Which infection is best managed with droplet precautions?

options.text: Influenza
Measles
Norovirus gastroenteritis
MRSA wound colonisation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: large respiratory droplets over a short distance.
distractorRationale.c: Norovirus is managed with contact precautions.

questions.explanation: Influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets that travel about 1-2 metres, so a surgical mask and a single room are used. Measles needs airborne precautions, while norovirus and MRSA are contact-transmitted.

questions.stem: During an investigation of a cluster of postoperative wound infections, which action should come first after the cluster is recognised?

options.text: Confirm the diagnoses and define a case, while starting immediate control measures
Wait for the molecular typing results before taking any action
Publish the findings in a journal
Close the hospital to all admissions

questions.correctOptionText: Confirm the diagnoses and define a case, while starting immediate control measures

distractorRationale.d: A blanket closure is disproportionate before the source is known.

questions.explanation: The investigation starts by confirming that the cases are real and defining what counts as a case. Simple control measures are started without waiting for proof of the source.

questions.stem: An infection control nurse observes 120 hand hygiene opportunities on a ward, and staff perform correct hand hygiene on 78 of them. Calculate the compliance as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Compliance = 78 / 120 x 100 = 65%. Audit with feedback is a core tool for improving hand hygiene.

questions.stem: In a 24-bed respiratory unit, 9 patients develop an influenza-like illness with fever and cough over one week, and all 24 patients were present throughout. Calculate the attack rate as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Attack rate = cases / population at risk = 9 / 24 = 0.375, or 37.5%. Comparing attack rates among exposed and unexposed groups helps identify the source.

questions.stem: List the five moments for hand hygiene and explain which of them mainly protect the patient and which protect the healthcare worker and the environment.
markingGuide: Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Moments 1 and 2 protect the patient; moments 3, 4 and 5 protect staff and prevent spread to other patients and surroundings
questions.explanation: The moments map to when hands are most likely to transmit organisms. Knowing the purpose of each makes them easier to apply.

questions.stem: Distinguish contact, droplet and airborne transmission-based precautions, giving one example infection and the key measures for each.
markingGuide: Contact: direct or indirect touch; example MRSA, C. difficile or norovirus; gloves, apron, single room, dedicated equipment
Droplet: large droplets over about 1-2 m; example influenza or meningococcus; surgical mask and single room
Airborne: small droplet nuclei that remain suspended over long distances; example TB, measles or chickenpox; negative-pressure room and FFP3/N95 respirator
Transmission-based precautions are added to standard precautions
questions.explanation: The route and particle size determine the barriers needed. Using a respirator and negative pressure only for airborne agents conserves resources.

questions.stem: A hospital notices six cases of the same Gram-negative bloodstream infection on an intensive care unit in ten days. Outline the steps you would take to investigate this as a possible outbreak.
markingGuide: Confirm the outbreak (compare to expected numbers) and verify diagnoses
Define a case and search actively for further cases
Describe by time (epidemic curve), place and person
Formulate a hypothesis about source and route (for example contaminated equipment or cross-infection)
Implement control measures immediately: isolation or cohorting, hand hygiene, environmental cleaning
Laboratory typing of isolates and analytic study; communicate and review
questions.explanation: A systematic approach prevents wasted effort and protects patients while evidence builds. Control measures begin early and are refined as the source becomes clear.
